A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same legislative lobbying testbed. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching analyses moved into v2's appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original lobbying simulations across six LLM configurations, with reinforcement, chain-of-thought, component-ablation, state, and policy-area results.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation results and adds stronger-critic experiments, benefit-capture measurements, structured human evaluations, and prompt robustness tests.

M1.justification: The pairwise critic, memory, critique, and self-reflection architecture remains. However, v2 reports top-one identification as the trigger for further reinforcement, versus v1's implemented top-two rule, changing when another revision is requested. The new benefit score evaluates outputs; it does not establish a new optimized training loss.

E1.justification: Both evaluate U.S. congressional-bill lobbying using roughly 4.5K bill-company pairs across 32 policy areas. The dataset is named LobbyLens in v2; Appendix A clarifies that 121 source companies yield 114 retained companies, matching v1's reported coverage. Added ratings and critic configurations evaluate the existing task rather than establish another target population or domain.

E2.justification: v2 adds a lobbyist baseline without concealment instructions and a critic variant using company names without descriptions (Table 5), compared with the standard configuration in Table 4. v1's chain-of-thought and no-reflection/no-critique comparators remain in v2 Tables 8-9. These are limited additions within the existing framework.

E3.justification: The main identification criterion changes from top-two to top-one, while top-two results remain in Appendix A. v2 adds stronger-critic configurations, a Qwen 72B benefit-capture metric, prompt tests on 10% of the dataset, and structured evaluations of 100 simulations by 10 raters; v1 described 100 informal spot-checks per model. The reported candidate range also changes from 4-11 to 4-12 companies per bill.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of benefit retention, human judgments of benefit substantialness and critique quality, stronger critics, prompt ordering and wording, and additional prompt ablations (Figures 2-3 and Tables 2-5). The state analysis gains a Squire Index comparison. Original chain-of-thought, component-ablation, and policy-area analyses survive in Appendix A.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without an uncertainty procedure. v2 introduces standard deviations and error bars from 10,000 bootstrap resamples for main identification, benefit-capture, and prompt experiments, plus inter-rater agreement reporting in Table 3. Bootstrap resampling does not establish an increase in independent model runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds top-one identification, stronger-critic, benefit-capture, human-rating, and prompt-control results. Table 2 newly reports Qwen 72B benefit capture declining from 96.1% to 83.5% across trials. Figure 2's 83.7%-to-41.3% identification trajectory uses top-one; v1's 92.1%-to-64.0% top-two trajectory remains in Table 6, so these are not same-setting performance gains. State rankings also change.

T1.justification: v2 adds formal definitions of declared and hidden intent, critic and benefit scores, a deception constraint (Equation 2), and a constrained expected-benefit objective (Equation 3). v1 only mathematically specified similarity-based dataset matching. This adds a limited formal formulation without new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central testbed contribution and claim that verbal reinforcement increases deception remain. v2 revises the headline from approximately 40% relative improvement to approximately 40 percentage points under the revised criterion, focuses its closing abstract claim on agent-to-agent manipulation, and adds a state-professionalism association in the introduction.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges benefit loss, critic weaknesses, the absence of human-target deception tests, and restricted applicability to amendment suggestions. It adds an interpretation of the tradeoff between evading identification and retaining benefits. The Nebraska/Louisiana explanations based on presumed training exposure are replaced by a qualitative Squire Index comparison and a proposed red-teaming application.

D1.justification: v2 supplies extensive prompts, filtering counts, tokenizer and embedding/reranking details, constrained-generation instructions, GGUF/llama.cpp information, two-A100/two-week compute requirements, and GPT-4 API costs. It also documents the source-data license and promises dataset release upon publication. These substantially extend v1's shorter prompts and high-level implementation description; the promise does not establish current availability.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around deception detection, communication and cognitive theories, and political-text measurement. Additions include Hagendorff (2024), Buller and Burgoon (1996), McCornack (2015), and Squire (2024), alongside an explicit dataset comparison with Nay (2023). v1's sweeping first-work assertion becomes an emphasis on underexplored subtle deception.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology, and analysis narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 removes the long rabbit-hat analogy, shortens the title, moves related work near the beginning, separates dataset construction from the framework, and reorganizes retained analyses into appendices. Dedicated limitations and ethics sections replace the earlier closing structure.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main paper to two columns, compacts and redraws the framework illustration, redesigns the main charts with consistent trial colors and uncertainty bars, and adds substantial new tables and a stronger-critic figure. v1's two-panel chain-of-thought/ablation figure becomes Appendix Tables 8-9, while the policy-area figure moves to the appendix.

improvement.justification: v1 primarily treats non-identification as deception and validates generated content through informal spot-checks. v2 materially strengthens this central inference by measuring retained benefits, adding structured human judgments and stronger-critic tests, and documenting uncertainty, prompts, and limitations. Reporting defects remain, notably Figure 3's caption reversing GPT-4's role relative to its axis label and explanatory text, but the substantial validation and reproducibility gains outweigh these inconsistencies.
